title: The vowels
hook: dots and dashes added by the Masoretes to show vowels

segments.voice: Yesterday, sofit: the five letters that change shape when a word ends. Your line was five endings. Did you write one? Today, a new week, and the little marks that make the letters speak. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-two.

Open a Torah scroll, the handwritten one kept in the ark of a synagogue, and look closely at the columns. Black letters, row after row, beautifully formed. And something missing. No dots under the letters. No little dashes. No marks above. Just consonants. The person reading aloud on a Sabbath morning has to know how each word sounds before they get there. So the reader prepares ahead of time, and one tool for that is a printed book laid out in two columns: the plain letters on one side, and on the other, the same words with tiny dots and lines added. Those tiny marks are today's word.
screen: `A TORAH SCROLL, UP CLOSE.` → `ONLY CONSONANTS.` → `A PRACTICE BOOK WITH THE MARKS.`

segments.voice: Nikud. The dots and dashes that show the vowels. Turn it four ways. First, the letters. Every letter we've learned this block, from alef to tav, is a consonant, or a silent letter like alef and ayin. Hebrew can be written with no vowels at all. A reader who knows the language fills the sounds in. Second, the marks. Scribes and scholars called the Masoretes worked out a system of small signs to fix how the sacred text was read aloud. A short line under a letter says ah. A single dot under it says ee. A dot above says oh. They sit around the letters without changing a single one. The letters stay exactly as the scribes wrote them; the marks only guide the voice. Third, why it matters. Some words share all their letters and differ only by vowels. Samech, peh, resh can be read sefer, a book, or sofer, a scribe. The dots tell you which. The Talmud, in tractate Nedarim, reads a verse from Nehemiah, where Ezra's helpers read the Torah to the people and "gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading," as pointing to the breaks and the chant of the text, the reading handed down with the letters. Fourth, where you'll meet them. These dots are scaffolding. Children learn with them. Prayer books print them. And a Torah reader carries them in memory, even when the scroll leaves them out.
screen: `ONLY CONSONANTS ON THE PAGE.` · `DOTS AND LINES FOR THE VOWELS.` · `SAME LETTERS, DIFFERENT WORDS.` · `SCAFFOLDING YOU CARRY IN MEMORY.` · then, large: `THE DOTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one vowel sound. Settle, and breathe. On the screen is bet, the letter of the house. With a short line under it, it reads ba. With a dot under it, bee. With a dot above, bo. Say each one quietly: ba, bee, bo. Then pick one and stay with it. Breathe in, and on the out breath, let the sound go. The letter stays still. Only the breath changes. If you pray, you can let one word of a prayer you know rest on your breath the same way. The bell holds the time.
Nikud. The vowel points: dots and lines around the letters, telling the voice how to read them. Today's word.
Your line: the dots. Today, when you read anything, notice how much you already fill in without being told. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Printed Hebrew Bibles and prayer books carry the vowel points, and children learn to read with them; the handwritten Torah scroll read in synagogue has no vowels, so the reader prepares in advance from a printed text that shows them.

original.note: Hebrew: the vowel points, the dots and lines added around the letters.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hebrew vowels are letters, like a, e and o.
what it means: the vowels are small dots and lines around the letters, and they can be left off.
what a scholar hears: the Masoretes added the marks without touching a letter of the text, so the written word and its spoken reading travel together.
